Construction & Demolition Recycling OrdinanceTo encourage construction and demolition recycling, the Town of Danville has adopted a construction and demolition recycling ordinance. The ordinance requires certain projects within the Town to divert 65% of their job debris from the landfill. The ordinance requires applicants to visit http://danville.wastetracking.com/ and submit:A Waste Management Plan (WMP) as part of the application submittal requirements for a building, grading, demolition or similar permitWeighmaster certificates for all debris recycling must be submitted to verify plan compliance prior to permit finalization.Applicable ProjectsWaste tracking per the town's Construction and Demolition Recycling Ordinance is required for the following types of construction projects:Commercial Additions, Demolitions, and New ConstructionTenant Improvements exceeding $200,000 in valuationResidential Additions, Demolitions, and New ConstructionResidential Alterations that increase the volume of living spaceThe following types of projects are exempt from the Construction and Demolition Recycling Ordinance:Cell SitesResidential Re-RoofsSwimming PoolsDetached Accessory StructuresResidential Remodels and Alterations within the existing footprint where no additional square footage or volume of living area are created.Mandatory Use of Certified Facilities In order to be counted toward the project’s 65% diversion requirement, all construction and demolition waste must be taken to a Certified Construction and Demolition Recovery Facility. These Certified Facilities will provide weighmaster certificates that must be uploaded to http://danville.wastetracking.com/  to verify compliance with the C&D Ordinance. What should I do if my garbage/recycling/organics collection is missed?
If your garbage, recycling, or organics collection is missed, you should call Republic Services at their toll-free number, (800) 320-8077, before 12 noon for a return trip on the same day.
do i need to pay for garbage/recycling/organics service? what if I do not have enough money?

Yes, you are required to pay for garbage, recycling, and organics service. According to the Piedmont Municipal Code, every property owner must ensure that arrangements are made for the proper disposal of solid waste, recyclable material, and organic waste. 

If you are concerned about the cost and do not have enough money, you may want to explore options to reduce your service costs, such as switching to a smaller garbage cart if you can recycle more and generate less garbage. Additionally, you can inquire about any available discounts or assistance programs that may help with the costs.
can you please clarify the service rate here?

I do not have specific information regarding the service rate for garbage, recycling, or organics collection. You may want to contact your local waste management service provider for detailed information on rates and any available assistance programs.
recycle food scraps

To recycle food scraps, you should collect them along with food-soiled paper in a designated green kitchen pail. Once the pail is full, empty its contents into the larger green Organics cart for collection. It's important not to place the kitchen pail outside for collection. This process helps divert food scraps from landfills, turning them into compost, which is a valuable resource for landscaping and farming. For more detailed information, you can refer to local guidelines or visit resources like the http://stopfoodwaste.org website.
I do not want to miss my garbage collection service again...especially during the holiday time

To avoid missing your garbage collection service during the holiday season, it's important to be aware of the collection schedule. There is no garbage, organics, or recycling collection on New Year's Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, and Christmas Day. When these holidays fall on a weekday, pickup is one day later for the rest of the week, including Saturday.

To ensure you don't miss your collection, you can:

1. **Check the holiday schedule**: Be aware of the specific holidays and how they affect your collection day.
2. **Set reminders**: Use a calendar or reminder app to alert you a day or two before your scheduled collection day, especially if it falls after a holiday.
3. **Place your carts out on time**: If you have curbside collection, make sure to place your carts within three feet of the curb no earlier than 6:00 p.m. the day before collection and remove them by midnight on the collection day.

By following these steps, you can help ensure that you don't miss your garbage collection service.
what is electronic waste and hazardous waste here?

**Electronic Waste (E-Waste)** refers to discarded electrical or electronic devices. This includes items such as computers, televisions, cell phones, tablets, printers, and other electronic equipment. E-waste can contain hazardous materials that can be harmful to the environment if not disposed of properly.

**Hazardous Waste** includes materials that are toxic, corrosive, ignitable, or reactive, and can pose a threat to human health and the environment if not managed correctly. Examples of hazardous waste include household products like paints, solvents, batteries, pesticides, and certain automotive fluids.

In Sierra County, CA, residents can dispose of both electronic waste and hazardous waste at designated solid waste sites. For electronic waste, it is accepted for free from residents at specific transfer stations. Hazardous waste is collected during an annual Household Hazardous Waste Event, typically held in October, where residents can bring items like antifreeze, batteries, oil, and paint for safe disposal.
how do I recycle paint?

To recycle paint, you should follow these guidelines:

1. **Latex Paint**: Latex paint is not considered hazardous waste. You can dispose of it by drying it out. To do this, remove the lid and add an absorbent material like kitty litter to the leftover paint. Allow the mixture to air dry until it hardens, and then you can throw the can in the garbage.

2. **Oil-Based Paint**: Oil-based paints must be taken to a designated drop-off location for proper disposal. You should not throw these in the regular trash. In many areas, you can take oil-based paint to an Alameda County Household Hazardous Waste Facility or a similar facility in your area.

3. **PaintCare Program**: Some regions have a PaintCare program that allows residents to drop off leftover oil-based and latex paints at specific locations for recycling. You can check for participating locations and accepted items by visiting the PaintCare website.

Make sure to check local regulations and guidelines for paint disposal, as they can vary by location.
I am allergic to latex...

If you are allergic to latex, here are some important steps you can take to protect yourself:

1. **Avoid Contact**: Stay away from natural rubber latex products, including gloves, balloons, and certain medical supplies.

2. **Use Non-Latex Alternatives**: If you need to wear gloves for work or other activities, ask your employer for non-latex gloves. 

3. **Avoid Powdered Latex Gloves**: If you are in environments where others may be using latex gloves, try to avoid areas where you might inhale the powder from those gloves, as it can become airborne and trigger an allergic reaction.

4. **Wear a Medical ID**: Consider wearing a personal medical emergency ID bracelet that indicates your latex allergy.

5. **Carry an Epinephrine Kit**: If prescribed by your physician, carry an emergency epinephrine kit in case of accidental exposure that leads to anaphylactic shock. Make sure that family members, friends, and coworkers know how to use it.

6. **Inform Healthcare Providers**: Always inform your healthcare providers about your latex allergy before any medical or dental procedures. It’s advisable to schedule appointments early in the day to minimize exposure to airborne latex particles.

7. **Educate Yourself and Others**: Participate in educational programs about latex allergy and inform those around you, including school or daycare providers if applicable.

8. **Work with Medical Professionals**: Collaborate with your allergist and local medical facilities to find latex-safe environments for treatment.

If you have any specific concerns or symptoms, it is important to consult with a physician experienced in diagnosing and managing latex allergies.

 This ordinance applies to certain businesses and institutions and requires plant debris be separated and composted. Alameda County law prohibits disposal of plant debris in county landfills. Those subscribing to 4 or more cubic yards of weekly on-site garbage service must place plant debris in the designated “organics” bin, and those who haul to their local facility must deposit plant debris in the disposal facility’s designated “clean green” area. Plant debris includes grass, leaves, shrubbery, vines and tree branches.
 This law applies to any person or organization generating significant amounts of plant debris that hauls the material to Alameda County disposal facilities or places the material in bins for collection, including:

Commercial and institutional (e.g. colleges, hospitals, park districts, golf courses) customers subscribing to 4 or more cubic yards of weekly solid waste collection service.
Landscapers and gardeners
Municipalities

and unincorporated areas in Alameda County.

retrieved_documents.text:
FAQs • Morgan Hill • CivicEngage
What if I don’t change anything about how I dispose of my waste?

Yes, everyone is required to participate. If you choose not to participate, you may receive an improper facility use fine as laid out by the State of California (Government Code Sections 53069.4, 25132, 36900). 

3.
Why are the requirements changing?

A focus on recovering and recycling organic materials is vital to California’s efforts to combat climate change. When organic materials such as food scraps, yard trimmings, and paper decompose anaerobically (without oxygen) in a landfill, they produce methane — one of the most potent climate pollutants in the atmosphere and a major contributor to climate change. 

4.
What are the fines for improper facility use? 

If self-haulers do not abide by the organic waste requirements as laid out by the State of California, they are subject to improper facility use fines. For violations occurring after January 1, 2024, the State of California requires all jurisdictions to issue a Notice of Violation requiring compliance within 60 days. If after 60 days, the entity is still not in compliance, the jurisdiction is required to impose penalties. The penalties imposed by any jurisdiction are based on Government Code Sections 53069.4, 25132 and 36900 and are as follows:First violation: $50-$100 per violationSecond violation: $100-$200 per violationThird or subsequent violation: $250-$500 per violation 

5.
Why is recycling organic waste important?

Organics recycling helps to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, improve air and water quality, and create valuable resources such as compost, renewable energy and mulch. In addition, it conserves natural resources by reducing the need for raw materials used in producing compost, mulch and renewable energy. This contributes to overall sustainability efforts and helps preserve ecosystems. 

6.
Are there additional resources available?

CalRecycle and local authorities may provide support and resources to help self-haulers understand and comply with SB 1383 requirements. This includes educational materials, training programs and tools such as the Record-keeping Tool for Self-Haulers, designed to facilitate compliance with record-keeping obligations.

retrieved_documents.text:
FAQs - City of Piedmont

The project supports local and regional efforts towards green- house gas reduction (climate change), oil independence, zero waste and landfill reduction.

Q. I'm interested in home composting. Where can I get more information?

A. Home composting information can be found on the StopWaste.org website.

I am interested in Recycling the Right Way

Q. Is recycling free?

A. Recycling is a weekly, unlimited service and included at no extra cost.

Q. What goes in the Blue Recycling Cart?

A. It's long list and includes all types of paper, flattened cardboard boxes, clean egg cartons and waxed paper containers, shredded paper, all plastics #1-7, aseptic containers, glass containers, metal/tin containers, aluminum foil/pans and empty spray cans, metal lids and caps. Click here to view Recycling details.

Q. What doesn't belong in the Blue Recycling Cart?

A. This is a long list too but anything that is trash, organics or household hazardous waste should not be placed in the Blue Cart. This includes ceramic plates/cups, window and mirror glass, light bulbs, glassware, metal coat hangers, clothing, snack wrappers, video/audio tapes, garden hoses, food products and more. Click here to view Recycling details.

Q. What if I have more recycling than what fits in my Blue Cart?

A. If you need an additional recycling cart, call Republic Services Customer Service at 800-320-8077. But if this is a one-time or occasional occurrence, your bagged recycling overage can be set out within 3 feet of the curb. However, notice is required!

Q. Where can I sell my California Redemption (CRV) containers?

A. Berkeley Recycling located at 669 Gilman Street in Berkeley pays for certain recyclables at their Buyback. To learn which materials will be purchased and current pricing, visit berkeleyrecycling.org.

Q. What is considered Electronic Waste(e-waste)?

A. If you need an additional recycling cart, call Republic Services Customer Service at 800-320-8077. But if this is a one-time or occasional occurrence, your bagged recycling overage can be set out within 3 feet of the curb. However, notice is required!

Q. Where can I sell my California Redemption (CRV) containers?

A. Berkeley Recycling located at 669 Gilman Street in Berkeley pays for certain recyclables at their Buyback. To learn which materials will be purchased and current pricing, visit berkeleyrecycling.org.

Q. What is considered Electronic Waste(e-waste)?

What should I do if my garbage/recycling/organics collection is missed?
If your garbage, recycling, or organics collection is missed, you should call Republic Services at their toll-free number, (800) 320-8077, before 12 noon for a return trip on the same day.
do i need to pay for garbage/recycling/organics service? what if I do not have enough money?

Yes, you are required to pay for garbage, recycling, and organics service. According to the Piedmont Municipal Code, every property owner must ensure that arrangements are made for the proper disposal of solid waste, recyclable material, and organic waste. 

If you are concerned about the cost and do not have enough money, you may want to explore options to reduce your service costs, such as switching to a smaller garbage cart if you can recycle more and generate less garbage. Additionally, you can inquire about any available discounts or assistance programs that may help with the costs.
can you please clarify the service rate here?

I do not have specific information regarding the service rate for garbage, recycling, or organics collection. You may want to contact your local waste management service provider for detailed information on rates and any available assistance programs.
recycle food scraps

To recycle food scraps, you should collect them along with food-soiled paper in a designated green kitchen pail. Once the pail is full, empty its contents into the larger green Organics cart for collection. It's important not to place the kitchen pail outside for collection. This process helps divert food scraps from landfills, turning them into compost, which is a valuable resource for landscaping and farming. For more detailed information, you can refer to local guidelines or visit resources like the http://stopfoodwaste.org website.
I do not want to miss my garbage collection service again...especially during the holiday time

To avoid missing your garbage collection service during the holiday season, it's important to be aware of the collection schedule. There is no garbage, organics, or recycling collection on New Year's Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, and Christmas Day. When these holidays fall on a weekday, pickup is one day later for the rest of the week, including Saturday.

To ensure you don't miss your collection, you can:

1. **Check the holiday schedule**: Be aware of the specific holidays and how they affect your collection day.
2. **Set reminders**: Use a calendar or reminder app to alert you a day or two before your scheduled collection day, especially if it falls after a holiday.
3. **Place your carts out on time**: If you have curbside collection, make sure to place your carts within three feet of the curb no earlier than 6:00 p.m. the day before collection and remove them by midnight on the collection day.

By following these steps, you can help ensure that you don't miss your garbage collection service.
what is electronic waste and hazardous waste here?

**Electronic Waste (E-Waste)** refers to discarded electrical or electronic devices. This includes items such as computers, televisions, cell phones, tablets, printers, and other electronic equipment. E-waste can contain hazardous materials that can be harmful to the environment if not disposed of properly.

**Hazardous Waste** includes materials that are toxic, corrosive, ignitable, or reactive, and can pose a threat to human health and the environment if not managed correctly. Examples of hazardous waste include household products like paints, solvents, batteries, pesticides, and certain automotive fluids.

In Sierra County, CA, residents can dispose of both electronic waste and hazardous waste at designated solid waste sites. For electronic waste, it is accepted for free from residents at specific transfer stations. Hazardous waste is collected during an annual Household Hazardous Waste Event, typically held in October, where residents can bring items like antifreeze, batteries, oil, and paint for safe disposal.
how do I recycle paint?

To recycle paint, you should follow these guidelines:

1. **Latex Paint**: Latex paint is not considered hazardous waste. You can dispose of it by drying it out. To do this, remove the lid and add an absorbent material like kitty litter to the leftover paint. Allow the mixture to air dry until it hardens, and then you can throw the can in the garbage.

2. **Oil-Based Paint**: Oil-based paints must be taken to a designated drop-off location for proper disposal. You should not throw these in the regular trash. In many areas, you can take oil-based paint to an Alameda County Household Hazardous Waste Facility or a similar facility in your area.

3. **PaintCare Program**: Some regions have a PaintCare program that allows residents to drop off leftover oil-based and latex paints at specific locations for recycling. You can check for participating locations and accepted items by visiting the PaintCare website.

Make sure to check local regulations and guidelines for paint disposal, as they can vary by location.
I am allergic to latex...

If you are allergic to latex, here are some important steps you can take to protect yourself:

1. **Avoid Contact**: Stay away from natural rubber latex products, including gloves, balloons, and certain medical supplies.

2. **Use Non-Latex Alternatives**: If you need to wear gloves for work or other activities, ask your employer for non-latex gloves. 

3. **Avoid Powdered Latex Gloves**: If you are in environments where others may be using latex gloves, try to avoid areas where you might inhale the powder from those gloves, as it can become airborne and trigger an allergic reaction.

4. **Wear a Medical ID**: Consider wearing a personal medical emergency ID bracelet that indicates your latex allergy.

5. **Carry an Epinephrine Kit**: If prescribed by your physician, carry an emergency epinephrine kit in case of accidental exposure that leads to anaphylactic shock. Make sure that family members, friends, and coworkers know how to use it.

6. **Inform Healthcare Providers**: Always inform your healthcare providers about your latex allergy before any medical or dental procedures. It’s advisable to schedule appointments early in the day to minimize exposure to airborne latex particles.

7. **Educate Yourself and Others**: Participate in educational programs about latex allergy and inform those around you, including school or daycare providers if applicable.

8. **Work with Medical Professionals**: Collaborate with your allergist and local medical facilities to find latex-safe environments for treatment.

If you have any specific concerns or symptoms, it is important to consult with a physician experienced in diagnosing and managing latex allergies.
if I plan to remodel my house, do I need to pay for the debris? can I move debris myself out from my house?

If you plan to remodel your house, you are required to manage the debris generated from the project. Here are the key points regarding debris management:

1. **Payment for Debris Removal**: You will need to pay for the removal of debris, as it is part of the overall costs associated with your remodeling project. However, there are no additional City fees specifically associated with the requirement to recycle construction and demolition (C&D) debris.

2. **Self-Hauling Debris**: You may self-haul the debris if you personally transport it to a solid waste and/or recycling facility. However, contractors or any paid haulers other than Republic Services cannot remove the debris for you. If you choose to self-haul, make sure to comply with the City’s regulations regarding debris disposal.

3. **Recycling Requirements**: If your remodeling project has a building permit valuation of $50,000 or more, you are required to divert at least 65% of the debris generated from going to a landfill. You are encouraged to salvage and reuse materials, and you will need to document this diversion to comply with the City’s regulations.

Make sure to check with local authorities or the City’s guidelines for any specific requirements or resources available for managing debris from your remodeling project.
I heard that Alameda County has three recycling ordinances that are mandatory. please explain with penalty.

turns.rag_answer:
Yes, Alameda County has three mandatory recycling ordinances aimed at reducing waste and promoting recycling and composting. Here’s a brief overview of each ordinance and the associated penalties for non-compliance:

1. **Organics Reduction and Recycling Ordinance**: This ordinance, implemented under California State law SB 1383, requires all generators of compostable and recyclable materials to keep food and other compostable materials out of landfills. Residents must sort compostable and recyclable materials into the appropriate containers. Businesses, nonprofits, institutions, schools, and multi-family properties must subscribe to compost and recycling collection services and inform their employees or tenants about the rules.

2. **Mandatory Commercial Recycling Law**: This law requires businesses and institutions with four or more cubic yards of garbage service, as well as multi-family properties with five or more units, to recycle. The law has been in effect since July 1, 2012, and mandates that businesses collect food scraps and compostable paper separately from garbage.

3. **Plant Debris Landfill Ban Ordinance**: This ordinance requires certain businesses and institutions to separate plant debris (like grass, leaves, and branches) from garbage and compost it instead. It applies to those subscribing to four or more cubic yards of weekly garbage service.

### Penalties for Non-Compliance:
If entities do not comply with these ordinances, they may face penalties. The penalties for violations can include:

- **First Violation**: Fines ranging from $50 to $100.
- **Second Violation**: Fines ranging from $100 to $200.
- **Third or Subsequent Violations**: Fines ranging from $250 to $500.

Additionally, jurisdictions are required to issue a Notice of Violation requiring compliance within 60 days. If compliance is not achieved within that timeframe, penalties will be imposed.

It is important for residents and businesses to understand these ordinances and comply to avoid fines and contribute to the overall goal of reducing waste in Alameda County.

reference.answer: Alameda County has indeed implemented three mandatory recycling ordinances: ORGANICS REDUCTION AND RECYCLING ORDINANCE, MANDATORY COMMERCIAL RECYCLING LAW, and PLANT DEBRIS LANDFILL BAN ORDINANCE. Violation of a City ordinance, such as the Construction and Demolition Debris Recycling Ordinance, is considered an infraction that may result in a fine.

Ordinances and Regulations
 With the passage of Assembly Bill 341 (Mandatory Commercial Recycling law) in 2011, California enacted a statewide program to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by diverting commercial solid waste from landfills. The law also established a statewide recycling goal of 75% by 2020. In 2016, AB 1826 (Mandatory Organics Recycling law) went into effect, requiring businesses and multifamily complexes that generated specified amounts of organic waste to arrange for organics collection services. Most recently, SB 1383 (California's Short-Lived Climate Pollutant Reduction law), in effect as of 2022, expanded upon the goals of AB 341 and AB 1826. 
 Alameda County has three recycling ordinances that are mandatory. The purpose of these ordinances is to reduce the amount of easily recyclable and compostable materials deposited in landfills from businesses, institutions, single-family and multi-family properties, and self-haulers. The ordinances are designed to help the state reach the long-term goal of reducing waste by ensuring that 75% of recyclables and compostables are diverted from the landfill by 2025. 
ORGANICS REDUCTION AND RECYCLING ORDINANCE 
California State law, SB 1383, aims to keep food and other compostable materials ("organics") out of landfills to reduce emissions that contribute to climate change. In Alameda County, the law is implemented and enforced under the Organics Reduction and Recycling Ordinance, which went into effect on January 1, 2022.

ORGANICS REDUCTION AND RECYCLING ORDINANCE 
California State law, SB 1383, aims to keep food and other compostable materials ("organics") out of landfills to reduce emissions that contribute to climate change. In Alameda County, the law is implemented and enforced under the Organics Reduction and Recycling Ordinance, which went into effect on January 1, 2022. The law affects all generators of compostable and recyclable materials; however, requirements may vary slightly for different generators. Residents must sort compostable and recyclable materials into the appropriate containers. Businesses, nonprofits, institutions, schools, and multi-family properties must: subscribe to compost (organics) and recycling collection service (or have an approved waiver on file); place color-coded labeled recycling and compost bins next to all garbage bins (not required in restrooms); and sort materials into the proper bins and inform employees, tenants, and contractors of the rules (at least annually and during move in and move out). In addition, some businesses that generate surplus edible food must recover and donate their surplus edible food and feed people. For more information, visit this page here.

Phase 2 of the Mandatory Recycling Ordinance began July 1, 2015 for all commercial accounts (regardless of garbage service volume).

PLANT DEBRIS LANDFILL BAN ORDINANCE
 This ordinance applies to certain businesses and institutions and requires plant debris be separated and composted. Alameda County law prohibits disposal of plant debris in county landfills. Plant Debris Landfill Ban Ordinance requires landscape professionals, residents and businesses to separate all plant debris from garbage. Those subscribing to 4 or more cubic yards of weekly on-site garbage service must place plant debris in the designated “organics” bin, and those who haul to their local facility must deposit plant debris in the disposal facility’s designated “clean green” area. Plant debris includes grass, leaves, shrubbery, vines and tree branches.
 This law applies to any person or organization generating significant amounts of plant debris that hauls the material to Alameda County disposal facilities or places the material in bins for collection, including:

Commercial and institutional (e.g. colleges, hospitals, park districts, golf courses) customers subscribing to 4 or more cubic yards of weekly solid waste collection service.
Landscapers and gardeners
Municipalities

City of Piedmont Construction and Demolition Debris Recycling FAQ 
More information on Piedmont Construction and Demolition Debris Recycling here. 
 Projects required by the California Green Building Standards (all newly constructed residential buildings and projects increasing the building's conditioned area, volume, or size) having a building permit valuation greater than or equal to $50,000 are required to divert at least 65% of the debris generated by the project from going to a landfill. This includes all construction, demolition and/or renovation projects within the City. Although not required, the City encourages projects with a valuation of less than $50,000 to recycle at least 65% of the debris generated.
 Q: Are there any additional City fees associated with these requirements?

Ordinances and Regulations - City of Piedmont

If you do salvage or reuse, you will need to submit a SMF along with weight estimates and receipts from salvage vendors to the City to document that you have diverted at least 65% of the C&D materials from the landfill. Please refer to the Builders’ Guide to Reuse & Recycling for information on salvage and reuse service providers.
 Q: How do I estimate the weight of materials reused or salvaged? 
 A: You should use the attached City approved Conversion Table for Salvage and Reuse to estimate the weight of these materials.
 Q: How do I comply with the Diversion Goal if more than 65% of the debris generated is not recyclable? 
 A: If unique circumstances make it infeasible for you to comply with the Diversion Goal, you may apply, in writing, to the Building Official for an exemption.
 Q: What is the penalty for not complying with the Ordinance? 
 A: Violation of a City ordinance, such as the Construction and Demolition Debris Recycling Ordinance, is considered an infraction that may result in a fine. 
 Q: Are these requirements necessary? 
 A: Yes. C&D debris represents a significant portion of the City’s overall waste stream. Keeping these materials out of landfills is an essential part of the City’s plan for: 
    - Fulfilling the City’s own environmental and waste reduction goals; and 
    - Complying with the State’s Integrated Waste Management Act.

turns.rag_answer:
To file a complaint with the state, you can follow these general steps based on the documents provided:

1. **Identify the Appropriate Agency**: Determine which state agency is relevant to your complaint. For example, if your complaint is about utilities, you would contact the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC). If it's a consumer issue in New York, you would reach out to the New York State Attorney General's Office.

2. **Choose the Right Category**: Each agency typically has specific categories for complaints. For instance, the CPUC allows complaints related to public safety, utility issues, transportation, and unauthorized service changes. The New York State Attorney General's Office has categories for consumer issues, housing, technology, healthcare, civil rights, and more.

3. **File the Complaint**: 
   - For the **California Public Utilities Commission**, you can file a complaint online through their website or contact them directly for assistance.
   - For the **New York State Attorney General**, you can file a complaint online through their website or call their Help Line at 1-800-771-7755 for guidance.

4. **Provide Necessary Information**: Be prepared to provide details about your complaint, including any relevant documentation or evidence.

5. **Follow Up**: After filing, you may want to check the status of your complaint if the agency provides that option.

If you need specific instructions for a particular state or type of complaint, please let me know!

If you cannot complete the form online or need additional assistance, you can call their OAG Help Line at 1-800-771-7755. Please note that patterns of complaints often help in allocating law enforcement resources, and filing a false complaint is punishable as a Class A Misdemeanor.

How do I file a complaint with the state?

To file a complaint with the state, you can follow these general steps based on the documents provided:

1. **Identify the Appropriate Agency**: Determine which state agency is relevant to your complaint. For example, if your complaint is about utilities, you would contact the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC). If it's a consumer issue in New York, you would reach out to the New York State Attorney General's Office.

2. **Choose the Right Category**: Each agency typically has specific categories for complaints. For instance, the CPUC allows complaints related to public safety, utility issues, transportation, and unauthorized service changes. The New York State Attorney General's Office has categories for consumer issues, housing, technology, healthcare, civil rights, and more.

3. **File the Complaint**: 
   - For the **California Public Utilities Commission**, you can file a complaint online through their website or contact them directly for assistance.
   - For the **New York State Attorney General**, you can file a complaint online through their website or call their Help Line at 1-800-771-7755 for guidance.

4. **Provide Necessary Information**: Be prepared to provide details about your complaint, including any relevant documentation or evidence.

5. **Follow Up**: After filing, you may want to check the status of your complaint if the agency provides that option.

If you need specific instructions for a particular state or type of complaint, please let me know!

Report Unsafe Conditions
If the situation is an immediate safety threat, please call 911.
If you are a whistleblower, you can report unsafe conditions — confidentially, if you prefer — to us in the following ways:

Call the whistleblower hotline at 1-800-649-7570

File a Whistleblower Complaint Online

All others can report unsafe conditions to us in the following ways:

Call the whistleblower hotline at 1-800-649-7570

E-mail safetyhotline@cpuc.ca.gov

Who is a “Whistleblower”?
A whistleblower who can be assisted by us is an employee, contractor, or subcontractor of a company regulated by us who reports their employer’s suspected unsafe, unlawful, or dishonest activity. Whistleblowers may report their claims internally to their company’s upper management or to the company’s ethics officer or externally to regulators responsible for regulating the company. A whistleblower’s inside knowledge of the suspected unlawful or dishonest activity may help us discover something we would otherwise not know. Whistleblowers can play a valuable role in helping us get needed evidence to support the claim.
What is the role of the Public Utilities Commission?
We regulate privately owned electric, natural gas, phone, water, railroad, rail transit, and passenger transportation companies.

How do I file a complaint with the state?

To file a complaint with the state, you can follow these general steps based on the documents provided:

1. **Identify the Appropriate Agency**: Determine which state agency is relevant to your complaint. For example, if your complaint is about utilities, you would contact the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC). If it's a consumer issue in New York, you would reach out to the New York State Attorney General's Office.

2. **Choose the Right Category**: Each agency typically has specific categories for complaints. For instance, the CPUC allows complaints related to public safety, utility issues, transportation, and unauthorized service changes. The New York State Attorney General's Office has categories for consumer issues, housing, technology, healthcare, civil rights, and more.

3. **File the Complaint**: 
   - For the **California Public Utilities Commission**, you can file a complaint online through their website or contact them directly for assistance.
   - For the **New York State Attorney General**, you can file a complaint online through their website or call their Help Line at 1-800-771-7755 for guidance.

4. **Provide Necessary Information**: Be prepared to provide details about your complaint, including any relevant documentation or evidence.

5. **Follow Up**: After filing, you may want to check the status of your complaint if the agency provides that option.

About the Office

 

As head of the Department of Law, the Attorney General is both the People's Lawyer and the state's chief legal officer. The Attorney General serves as the guardian of the legal rights of the people of New York, its organizations, and its natural resources. As the state's chief legal counsel, the Attorney General advises the executive branch of state government, and defends actions and proceedings on behalf of the state.

 
Meet Letitia James 

The Attorney General serves the public interest of all New Yorkers in matters affecting their daily lives, enforcing laws to protect consumers, tenants, patients, workers, investors, and charitable donors. The office coordinates statewide civil and criminal investigations, promoting economic and social justice, encouraging harm-reducing public health strategies, and preserving the state’s environment. 
While the Attorney General acts independently of the Governor, the Governor or a state agency may request the Attorney General to undertake specific criminal investigations and prosecutions. The Attorney General's authority also includes the activities and investigations of the Organized Crime Task Force and Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.
The office employs over 1,700 staff, including investigators, analysts, scientists, forensic accountants, legal assistants and support staff, and over 700 assistant attorneys general, serving in over two dozen locations across New York state.

Administration Division | New York State Attorney General
The Office of Diversity and Inclusion provides leadership and guidance with respect to all diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) matters within our office.
With the goal of fostering DEIA, in 2020 the Attorney General established the Diversity Committee. The Diversity Committee is made up of 18 members, with two members representing each of the nine divisions at the office. The Diversity Committee works with the office to increase recruitment and hiring of a diverse workforce, enhance employee engagement and retention, and foster inclusion and equity within all aspects of the office.
Attorney General James is committed to providing a diverse, equitable, inclusive, accessible, and respectful environment for all employees and clients of the Office of the New York State Attorney General.

Practice Technologies Group
The Practice Technologies Group (PTG) provides litigation support and discovery services to the attorneys and legal support staff of the Office of the New York State Attorney General. PTG’s offering includes data collection and search consulting, data processing and hosting, analytics and technology-assisted review, review strategy and project management, and trial-presentation services.

Meet Letitia James | New York State Attorney General
She protected New Yorkers’ health and the state’s natural resources by going after polluters and companies that flouted environmental protection laws. Attorney General James stood up for vulnerable populations by going all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court to stop a question about citizenship from being added to the census and successfully protecting DACA. 
She has been a national leader in the fight to defend access to reproductive health care, leading dozens of legal actions across the country to protect and expand access to this lifesaving care. Attorney General James also stood up against corruption and took strong action against officials who broke New York laws or workplace protection measure, regardless of their status or political affiliation.  

Before serving as Attorney General, Letitia James was the public advocate for the City of New York. When she was elected in 2013, she became the first woman of color to hold citywide office. During her tenure as public advocate, her office passed more legislation than all previous public advocates combined, including a groundbreaking law that banned questions about salary history from the employment process to address the pervasive gender wage gap. Prior to serving as public advocate, Letitia James represented the 35th Council District in Brooklyn in the New York City Council for 10 years. As a council member, she passed the Safe Housing Act, legislation that forced landlords to improve living conditions for tenants in New York City’s worst buildings. Before her election to the City Council, Letitia James was head of the Brooklyn Regional Office of the New York State Attorney General’s Office. 
Letitia James began her career as a public defender at the Legal Aid Society. A proud Brooklynite, she is a graduate of Lehman College and Howard University School of Law.

Meet Letitia James

 

Letitia “Tish” James is the 67th Attorney General for the state of New York. With decades of experience and a long record of achievements, she is a powerful, effective attorney and lifelong public servant. When she was elected in 2018, she became the first woman of color to hold statewide office in New York and the first woman to be elected Attorney General. 

 
View the 2022 Year in Review 

In her first term, Attorney General James focused on protecting vulnerable New York residents and ensuring that individuals or companies that broke state laws were held accountable. She secured more than $7.5 billion for New York from those who broke state laws and took advantage of New Yorkers, including more than $2.5 billion from opioid manufacturers and distributors for their roles in the opioid epidemic. Under her leadership, the Office of the New York State Attorney General helped remove more than 4,000 guns from New York communities, took down dozens of dangerous drug and gun trafficking rings throughout the state, and took legal action to stop the proliferation of ghost guns.
Attorney General James took on predatory landlords who harassed tenants and endangered children by violating New York’s lead paint laws. She protected New Yorkers’ health and the state’s natural resources by going after polluters and companies that flouted environmental protection laws. Attorney General James stood up for vulnerable populations by going all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court to stop a question about citizenship from being added to the census and successfully protecting DACA. 
She has been a national leader in the fight to defend access to reproductive health care, leading dozens of legal actions across the country to protect and expand access to this lifesaving care.

- She began her career as a public defender at the Legal Aid Society.

**Career:**
- Before becoming Attorney General, James served as the Public Advocate for the City of New York, where she was the first woman of color to hold citywide office. During her tenure, she passed more legislation than all previous public advocates combined, including a significant law banning salary history questions in the employment process to combat the gender wage gap.
- Prior to her role as Public Advocate, she represented the 35th Council District in Brooklyn in the New York City Council for ten years, where she passed the Safe Housing Act to improve living conditions for tenants.
- She also worked as the head of the Brooklyn Regional Office of the New York State Attorney General’s Office.

**Achievements as Attorney General:**
- James has focused on protecting vulnerable populations and holding individuals and companies accountable for breaking state laws. 
- She has secured over $7.5 billion for New York from those who violated state laws, including more than $2.5 billion from opioid manufacturers and distributors related to the opioid epidemic.
- Under her leadership, the office has taken significant actions to remove guns from communities, combat drug and gun trafficking, and address issues related to predatory landlords and environmental protection.
- She has been a national leader in defending access to reproductive health care and has taken legal actions to protect and expand access to this essential care.

Letitia James is recognized for her commitment to social justice, consumer protection, and environmental advocacy, making her a prominent figure in New York's legal and political landscape.

About the Office

 

As head of the Department of Law, the Attorney General is both the People's Lawyer and the state's chief legal officer. The Attorney General serves as the guardian of the legal rights of the people of New York, its organizations, and its natural resources. As the state's chief legal counsel, the Attorney General advises the executive branch of state government, and defends actions and proceedings on behalf of the state.

 
Meet Letitia James 

The Attorney General serves the public interest of all New Yorkers in matters affecting their daily lives, enforcing laws to protect consumers, tenants, patients, workers, investors, and charitable donors. The office coordinates statewide civil and criminal investigations, promoting economic and social justice, encouraging harm-reducing public health strategies, and preserving the state’s environment. 
While the Attorney General acts independently of the Governor, the Governor or a state agency may request the Attorney General to undertake specific criminal investigations and prosecutions. The Attorney General's authority also includes the activities and investigations of the Organized Crime Task Force and Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.
The office employs over 1,700 staff, including investigators, analysts, scientists, forensic accountants, legal assistants and support staff, and over 700 assistant attorneys general, serving in over two dozen locations across New York state.

Administration Division | New York State Attorney General
The Office of Diversity and Inclusion provides leadership and guidance with respect to all diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) matters within our office.
With the goal of fostering DEIA, in 2020 the Attorney General established the Diversity Committee. The Diversity Committee is made up of 18 members, with two members representing each of the nine divisions at the office. The Diversity Committee works with the office to increase recruitment and hiring of a diverse workforce, enhance employee engagement and retention, and foster inclusion and equity within all aspects of the office.
Attorney General James is committed to providing a diverse, equitable, inclusive, accessible, and respectful environment for all employees and clients of the Office of the New York State Attorney General.

Practice Technologies Group
The Practice Technologies Group (PTG) provides litigation support and discovery services to the attorneys and legal support staff of the Office of the New York State Attorney General. PTG’s offering includes data collection and search consulting, data processing and hosting, analytics and technology-assisted review, review strategy and project management, and trial-presentation services.

The OAG is committed to community outreach and education, providing resources and information to help New Yorkers understand their rights and access legal services. The office also sponsors initiatives to promote public health and safety.

About the Office

 

As head of the Department of Law, the Attorney General is both the People's Lawyer and the state's chief legal officer. The Attorney General serves as the guardian of the legal rights of the people of New York, its organizations, and its natural resources. As the state's chief legal counsel, the Attorney General advises the executive branch of state government, and defends actions and proceedings on behalf of the state.

 
Meet Letitia James 

The Attorney General serves the public interest of all New Yorkers in matters affecting their daily lives, enforcing laws to protect consumers, tenants, patients, workers, investors, and charitable donors. The office coordinates statewide civil and criminal investigations, promoting economic and social justice, encouraging harm-reducing public health strategies, and preserving the state’s environment. 
While the Attorney General acts independently of the Governor, the Governor or a state agency may request the Attorney General to undertake specific criminal investigations and prosecutions. The Attorney General's authority also includes the activities and investigations of the Organized Crime Task Force and Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.

How do I file a complaint with the state?

To file a complaint with the state, you can follow these general steps based on the documents provided:

1. **Identify the Appropriate Agency**: Determine which state agency is relevant to your complaint. For example, if your complaint is about utilities, you would contact the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC). If it's a consumer issue in New York, you would reach out to the New York State Attorney General's Office.

2. **Choose the Right Category**: Each agency typically has specific categories for complaints. For instance, the CPUC allows complaints related to public safety, utility issues, transportation, and unauthorized service changes. The New York State Attorney General's Office has categories for consumer issues, housing, technology, healthcare, civil rights, and more.

3. **File the Complaint**: 
   - For the **California Public Utilities Commission**, you can file a complaint online through their website or contact them directly for assistance.
   - For the **New York State Attorney General**, you can file a complaint online through their website or call their Help Line at 1-800-771-7755 for guidance.

4. **Provide Necessary Information**: Be prepared to provide details about your complaint, including any relevant documentation or evidence.

5. **Follow Up**: After filing, you may want to check the status of your complaint if the agency provides that option.

can you please tell me more about Letitia James?

Letitia "Tish" James is the 67th Attorney General of the state of New York, having been elected to the position in 2018. She made history as the first woman of color to hold statewide office in New York and the first woman to be elected Attorney General. 

**Background and Education:**
- Letitia James is a proud Brooklynite and graduated from Lehman College and Howard University School of Law.
- She began her career as a public defender at the Legal Aid Society.

**Career:**
- Before becoming Attorney General, James served as the Public Advocate for the City of New York, where she was the first woman of color to hold citywide office. During her tenure, she passed more legislation than all previous public advocates combined, including a significant law banning salary history questions in the employment process to combat the gender wage gap.
- Prior to her role as Public Advocate, she represented the 35th Council District in Brooklyn in the New York City Council for ten years, where she passed the Safe Housing Act to improve living conditions for tenants.
- She also worked as the head of the Brooklyn Regional Office of the New York State Attorney General’s Office.

**Achievements as Attorney General:**
- James has focused on protecting vulnerable populations and holding individuals and companies accountable for breaking state laws. 
- She has secured over $7.5 billion for New York from those who violated state laws, including more than $2.5 billion from opioid manufacturers and distributors related to the opioid epidemic.
- Under her leadership, the office has taken significant actions to remove guns from communities, combat drug and gun trafficking, and address issues related to predatory landlords and environmental protection.
- She has been a national leader in defending access to reproductive health care and has taken legal actions to protect and expand access to this essential care.

Letitia James is recognized for her commitment to social justice, consumer protection, and environmental advocacy, making her a prominent figure in New York's legal and political landscape.
wow, that sounds great. maybe tell me more about Office of the New York State Attorney General itself

The Office of the New York State Attorney General (OAG) serves as the chief legal office for the state of New York, with a mission to protect the legal rights of the people, organizations, and natural resources of the state. Here are some key aspects of the office:

### Structure and Divisions
The OAG is organized into several divisions, each focusing on different areas of law and public service:

1. **Administration Division**: Manages the internal operations of the office, including human resources, budget, and information technology.

2. **Criminal Justice Division**: Handles criminal investigations and prosecutions, including the Conviction Review Bureau and the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.

3. **Economic Justice Division**: Focuses on consumer protection, antitrust issues, and investor protection, ensuring fair economic practices.

4. **Social Justice Division**: Works on civil rights, housing protection, environmental issues, and labor rights, advocating for marginalized communities.

5. **Solicitor General Division**: Manages appeals and legal opinions, representing the state in significant legal matters.

6. **State Counsel Division**: Provides legal representation for state agencies and handles civil recoveries and claims.

7. **Regional Offices**: The OAG has 13 regional offices across New York, which help carry out the office's functions in various parts of the state, including litigation, consumer protection, and community outreach.

### Mission and Responsibilities
- **Public Interest**: The Attorney General serves as the "People's Lawyer," advocating for the public interest in various legal matters affecting New Yorkers' daily lives.
- **Legal Representation**: The office represents the state in legal matters, providing counsel to state agencies and defending state laws.
- **Consumer Protection**: The OAG enforces laws to protect consumers, tenants, patients, workers, and investors from fraud and abuse.
- **Social Justice**: The office promotes social and economic justice, addressing issues such as discrimination, housing rights, and environmental protection.
- **Criminal Justice**: The OAG investigates and prosecutes criminal activities, including organized crime and Medicaid fraud.

### Community Engagement
The OAG is committed to community outreach and education, providing resources and information to help New Yorkers understand their rights and access legal services. The office also sponsors initiatives to promote public health and safety.

### Leadership
Letitia James, as the Attorney General, leads the office and is dedicated to ensuring that it operates effectively and fairly, with a focus on diversity, equity, and inclusion within the workplace.

Letitia "Tish" James is the 67th Attorney General of the state of New York, having been elected to the position in 2018. She made history as the first woman of color to hold statewide office in New York and the first woman to be elected Attorney General. 

**Background and Education:**
- Letitia James is a proud Brooklynite and graduated from Lehman College and Howard University School of Law.
- She began her career as a public defender at the Legal Aid Society.

**Career:**
- Before becoming Attorney General, James served as the Public Advocate for the City of New York, where she was the first woman of color to hold citywide office. During her tenure, she passed more legislation than all previous public advocates combined, including a significant law banning salary history questions in the employment process to combat the gender wage gap.
- Prior to her role as Public Advocate, she represented the 35th Council District in Brooklyn in the New York City Council for ten years, where she passed the Safe Housing Act to improve living conditions for tenants.
- She also worked as the head of the Brooklyn Regional Office of the New York State Attorney General’s Office.

**Achievements as Attorney General:**
- James has focused on protecting vulnerable populations and holding individuals and companies accountable for breaking state laws. 
- She has secured over $7.5 billion for New York from those who violated state laws, including more than $2.5 billion from opioid manufacturers and distributors related to the opioid epidemic.

retrieved_documents.text:
Whistleblower Protection - NASA OIG
Current and former Federal civilian employees and applicants can confidentially report information to an OIG or OSC about any of the following types of wrongdoing:

a violation of any law, rule, or regulation;
mismanagement;
a gross waste of funds;
an abuse of authority; or
a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety.
Censorship related to scientific research, analysis, or technology (scientific integrity)

Can I keep my identity confidential?
Yes. NASA OIG has a hotline that allows employees to make confidential disclosures. Inspectors General are prohibited from disclosing an employee’s identity without the employee’s consent unless the IG determines that disclosure is unavoidable or is compelled by a court order. If you file a disclosure with OSC, your identity will not be shared outside OSC without your consent. OSC may disclose your identity only if OSC determines that it is necessary because of an imminent danger to public health or safety or an imminent violation of any criminal law.
Are whistleblowers protected from retaliation?
Yes. The Whistleblower Protection Act prohibits retaliation. This means it is unlawful for agencies to take or threaten to take a personnel action against an employee because he or she disclosed wrongdoing. Personnel actions can include poor performance review, demotion, suspension, termination, or revocation or downgrade of a security clearance.In addition, the law prohibits retaliation for:

filing an appeal, complaint, or grievance;
helping someone else file or testifying on that person’s behalf;
cooperating with or disclosing information to OSC or an Inspector General; or
refusing to obey an unlawful order.

Are disclosures to Congress protected?
Yes. Federal law establishes that a Federal employee has the right to communicate with and provide information to the United States Congress.
What can you do if you believe whistleblower retaliation occurred?
If you believe that an agency has retaliated against you because of your whistleblowing, you can:

file a complaint with OSC, which may seek corrective action when warranted;
file a union grievance; or

We do not have final control over whether your identity is revealed. A Commission action or a court of law could decide that, in a particular situation, showing your identity would be in the public interest.
Are Whistleblowers protected by the law?
Yes. California Labor Code Section 1102.5(b) protects you from retaliation by your employer if you have reasonable cause to believe that the information reveals a violation of or noncompliance with state or federal statute, rule, or regulation.
Government Code Section 12653 reads, in part, “No employer shall discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, harass, deny promotion to, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee because of lawful acts in disclosing information to a government agency.”
We support these protections and expect the companies we regulate to obey the law. Although these laws are intended to protect you, you may still face the risk of retaliation. You may have to dedicate your personal time and money to hire an attorney to file a lawsuit for retaliation.

As a potential whistleblower, you should determine if your employer has set up internal procedures to handle whistleblower claims. If so, you should review these procedures to figure out how to proceed.

You are not protected from retaliation if you break the confidentiality of the lawyer-client privilege. (Labor Code section 1102.5(g)). So, you should not reveal any privileged information. Also, California law does not protect disclosures made by private-sector whistleblowers that reveal a trade secret. Whistleblower laws generally do not protect you when your claims involve personal matters rather than public concern.
Whom should a Whistleblower contact?
You can contact us by phone, email, or reporting online. You can use any one of the following contacts, depending on what you are reporting. Please be ready to give enough information to support your claims of supposed improper or unlawful behavior. If this information is not given to us, we will not be able to help you in your case.
If the situation poses an immediate safety threat, please call 911!

a violation of any law, rule, or regulation;

You may also consult the web site of the U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC), or review this OSC pamphlet, Know Your Rights When Reporting Wrongs.
HOW TO MAKE A PROTECTED DISCLOSURE
It is unlawful for your employer to retaliate against you for making a “protected disclosure.” A disclosure is protected if it meets two criteria:

The disclosure must be based on a reasonable belief that wrongdoing has occurred. As explained in the chart below, the definition of wrongdoing varies slightly depending on your place of employment.
The disclosure must also be made to a person or entity that is authorized to receive it. Employees who reasonably believe they have evidence of wrongdoing are always protected for submitting that information to the OIG Hotline or your local OIG office. However, as explained in the chart below, the other authorized audiences are different, depending on your employment status.

StatusWrongdoing DefinedAuthorized AudiencesNASA EmployeesViolation of any law, rule or regulation; Gross mismanagement; Gross waste of funds; Abuse of authority; and substantial and specific danger to public health or safety. Censorship related to scientific research, analysis, or technology (scientific integrity)In general, employees may disclose information to anyone, including non-governmental audiences, unless the information is classified or specifically prohibited by law from release. However, if the information is classified or specifically prohibited by law from release, it may only be shared with the OIG, OSC, or a designated agency official.Contractors, Subcontractors, Grantees, Sub-grantees, and Personal Services ContractorsGross mismanagement of a Federal contract or grant;Gross waste of Federal funds,Abuse of authority relating to a Federal contract or grant,Substantial and specific danger to public health or safety, or violation of law, rule, or regulation related to a NASA contract (including the competition for or negotiation of a contract) or grant.For all disclosures, classified or unclassified, an employee of a contractor or grantee is only protected if the disclosure is made to: A Member of Congress or a representative of a committee of Congress. An Inspector General. The Government Accountability Office. A NASA employee responsible for contract or grant oversight or management at the relevant agency.

Letitia "Tish" James is the 67th Attorney General of the state of New York, having been elected to the position in 2018. She made history as the first woman of color to hold statewide office in New York and the first woman to be elected Attorney General. 

**Background and Education:**
- Letitia James is a proud Brooklynite and graduated from Lehman College and Howard University School of Law.
- She began her career as a public defender at the Legal Aid Society.

**Career:**
- Before becoming Attorney General, James served as the Public Advocate for the City of New York, where she was the first woman of color to hold citywide office. During her tenure, she passed more legislation than all previous public advocates combined, including a significant law banning salary history questions in the employment process to combat the gender wage gap.
- Prior to her role as Public Advocate, she represented the 35th Council District in Brooklyn in the New York City Council for ten years, where she passed the Safe Housing Act to improve living conditions for tenants.
- She also worked as the head of the Brooklyn Regional Office of the New York State Attorney General’s Office.

**Achievements as Attorney General:**
- James has focused on protecting vulnerable populations and holding individuals and companies accountable for breaking state laws. 
- She has secured over $7.5 billion for New York from those who violated state laws, including more than $2.5 billion from opioid manufacturers and distributors related to the opioid epidemic.
- Under her leadership, the office has taken significant actions to remove guns from communities, combat drug and gun trafficking, and address issues related to predatory landlords and environmental protection.
- She has been a national leader in defending access to reproductive health care and has taken legal actions to protect and expand access to this essential care.

Letitia James is recognized for her commitment to social justice, consumer protection, and environmental advocacy, making her a prominent figure in New York's legal and political landscape.

The Office of the New York State Attorney General (OAG) serves as the chief legal office for the state of New York, with a mission to protect the legal rights of the people, organizations, and natural resources of the state. Here are some key aspects of the office:

### Structure and Divisions
The OAG is organized into several divisions, each focusing on different areas of law and public service:

1. **Administration Division**: Manages the internal operations of the office, including human resources, budget, and information technology.

4. **Social Justice Division**: Works on civil rights, housing protection, environmental issues, and labor rights, advocating for marginalized communities.

6. **State Counsel Division**: Provides legal representation for state agencies and handles civil recoveries and claims.

The OAG is committed to community outreach and education, providing resources and information to help New Yorkers understand their rights and access legal services. The office also sponsors initiatives to promote public health and safety.

how can I protect myself if I am the whistleblower....

turns.rag_answer:
If you are a whistleblower, there are several steps you can take to protect yourself and ensure that your rights are upheld:

1. **Understand Your Rights**: Familiarize yourself with the laws that protect whistleblowers. In the United States, the Whistleblower Protection Act prohibits retaliation against federal employees who disclose information about wrongdoing. Additionally, many states have their own whistleblower protection laws.

2. **Confidential Reporting**: Use confidential reporting channels to disclose wrongdoing. For example, you can report to the Office of Inspector General (OIG) or the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) while maintaining your anonymity. These offices are required to keep your identity confidential unless disclosure is unavoidable.

3. **Document Everything**: Keep detailed records of any wrongdoing you witness, including dates, times, locations, and the individuals involved. Document your communications regarding the issue, including any reports you make and responses you receive.

4. **Seek Legal Advice**: Consider consulting with an attorney who specializes in whistleblower protection. They can provide guidance on your rights, help you navigate the reporting process, and advise you on how to handle potential retaliation.

5. **Avoid Disclosing Privileged Information**: Be cautious not to disclose any information that may violate attorney-client privilege or reveal trade secrets, as this could undermine your protection.

6. **Know the Reporting Channels**: Familiarize yourself with the appropriate channels for reporting wrongdoing within your organization and externally. This may include internal reporting procedures, state agencies, or federal offices.

7. **Be Prepared for Retaliation**: Understand that despite protections, some whistleblowers may still face retaliation. If you experience retaliation, document it and consider filing a complaint with the OSC or your agency's human resources department.

8. **Engage Support Networks**: Connect with whistleblower advocacy groups or support networks that can provide resources, guidance, and emotional support throughout the process.

9. **Stay Professional**: Maintain professionalism in your workplace interactions, even if you face hostility or retaliation. This can help protect your reputation and strengthen your case if you need to take legal action.

By taking these steps, you can better protect yourself as a whistleblower and ensure that your disclosures are handled appropriately.

The spacecraft dives through an approximately 1,500-mile-wide (2,400-kilometer-wide) gap between Saturn and its rings for the first time on April 26 and loops around to shoot through that gap another 21 times before ending its mission by burning up in the skies of Saturn on Sept. 15, 2017. Data from Cassini's grand finale provide insight into the planet's internal structure, rings, radiation environment and atmosphere (including the first direct measurements).
› visit website for more info

FEBRUARY 22, 2017First System of Seven Earth-Sized Planets Around a Single Star RevealedSpitzer Space Telescope

Forty light-years away, a system of seven Earth-sized planets encircle an ultra-cool dwarf star called TRAPPIST-1. This is the only known planetary system apart from our own that has three planets in the habitable zone, the area around a star in which a planet could support liquid water on its surface. In collaboration with several ground-based telescopes, including the Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope (TRAPPIST) in Chile, NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope helped reveal the number and nature of these planets, using its infrared vision.
› visit website for more info

JULY 4, 2016First Solar-Powered Spacecraft at JupiterJuno

After traveling 1.7 billion miles (2.7 billion kilometers) and nearly five years, Juno successfully begins orbiting the solar system's largest planet on Independence Day. It is the first solar-powered spacecraft to explore Jupiter and carries instruments that will enable it to peer down through the clouds and into the planet's interior, giving scientists clues about how Jupiter was born and how the entire solar system evolved.
› visit website for more info

MARCH 6, 2015First Spacecraft to Visit a Dwarf Planet and First Spacecraft to Orbit Two Planetary DestinationsDawn

Two-and-a-half years after it left its first destination, the protoplanet Vesta, NASA's Dawn spacecraft slips into orbit around Ceres, the largest world in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The spacecraft is approximately 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) from Ceres when it is captured by Ceres' gravity.

 About the mission On August 5, 2011, NASA’s Juno spacecraft embarked on a 5-year journey to Jupiter, our solar system's largest planet. Juno arrived at Jupiter on July 4, 2016, after a five-year, 1,740-million-mile journey, and settled into a 53-day polar orbit stretching from just above Jupiter’s cloud tops to the outer reaches of the Jovian magnetosphere.During the prime mission’s 35 orbits of Jupiter, Juno collected more than three terabits of science data and provided dazzling views of Jupiter and its satellites, all processed by citizen scientists with NASA’s first-ever camera dedicated to public outreach. Juno’s many discoveries have changed our view of Jupiter’s atmosphere and interior, revealing an atmospheric weather layer that extends far beyond its water clouds and a deep interior with a dilute heavy element core. Near the end of the prime mission, as the spacecraft’s orbit evolved, flybys of the moon Ganymede initiated Juno’s transition into a full Jovian system explorer.Now in its extended mission, Juno will continue its investigation of the solar system’s largest planet through September 2025, or until the spacecraft’s end of life.

DECEMBER 8, 1995First Jupiter OrbiterGalileo

After a five-year voyage, the Galileo spacecraft arrives at Jupiter.
Galileo is the first spacecraft to directly measure Jupiter's atmosphere with a descent probe, and conducts long-term observations of the Jovian system. After discoveries including evidence for the existence of a saltwater ocean beneath the Jovian moon Europa's icy surface, extensive volcanic processes on the moon Io and a magnetic field generated by the moon Ganymede, Galileo plunges into Jupiter's atmosphere on September 21, 2003 to prevent an unwanted impact with Europa.
› visit website for more info

MAY 25, 1993First Mission to Use 'Aerobraking' and Crash Intentionally Into a PlanetMagellan

Magellan, a spacecraft with a sophisticated imaging radar that eventually makes the most highly detailed maps of Venus ever captured, is the first spacecraft to test a new maneuvering technique that uses the planet's atmosphere to slow or steer a spacecraft. This technique, known as aerobraking, makes the orbit around Venus more circular so Magellan can collect better gravity data. Flight controllers first attempt the maneuver on May 25, 1993 (after the mission's fourth mapping cycle of Venus) and dip Magellan into Venus's atmosphere on each orbit until Aug. 3, 1993. On Oct. 12, 1994, Magellan also becomes the first spacecraft intentionally crashed into a planet. Flight controllers chose this trajectory so that Magellan could gather valuable data on Venus's atmosphere.
› visit website for more info

OCTOBER 29, 1991First Asteroid FlybyGalileo

While its ultimate destination is Jupiter and its mysterious moons, the Galileo mission also becomes notable for discoveries during its journey to the gas giant. It is the first spacecraft to visit an asteroid, called Gaspra. Galileo also provides the only close observations of a comet colliding with a planet when it witnesses fragments of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 impact Jupiter. And its flight past Venus in 1990 yields fascinating infrared images of the planet's clouds.

Forty light-years away, a system of seven Earth-sized planets encircle an ultra-cool dwarf star called TRAPPIST-1. This is the only known planetary system apart from our own that has three planets in the habitable zone, the area around a star in which a planet could support liquid water on its surface. DECEMBER 8, 1995First Jupiter OrbiterGalileo

After a five-year voyage, the Galileo spacecraft arrives at Jupiter.
Galileo is the first spacecraft to directly measure Jupiter's atmosphere with a descent probe, and conducts long-term observations of the Jovian system. After discoveries including evidence for the existence of a saltwater ocean beneath the Jovian moon Europa's icy surface, extensive volcanic processes on the moon Io and a magnetic field generated by the moon Ganymede, Galileo plunges into Jupiter's atmosphere on September 21, 2003 to prevent an unwanted impact with Europa.
› visit website for more info

MAY 25, 1993First Mission to Use 'Aerobraking' and Crash Intentionally Into a PlanetMagellan

Magellan, a spacecraft with a sophisticated imaging radar that eventually makes the most highly detailed maps of Venus ever captured, is the first spacecraft to test a new maneuvering technique that uses the planet's atmosphere to slow or steer a spacecraft. This technique, known as aerobraking, makes the orbit around Venus more circular so Magellan can collect better gravity data. Flight controllers first attempt the maneuver on May 25, 1993 (after the mission's fourth mapping cycle of Venus) and dip Magellan into Venus's atmosphere on each orbit until Aug. 3, 1993. On Oct. 12, 1994, Magellan also becomes the first spacecraft intentionally crashed into a planet. Flight controllers chose this trajectory so that Magellan could gather valuable data on Venus's atmosphere.
› visit website for more info

OCTOBER 29, 1991First Asteroid FlybyGalileo

While its ultimate destination is Jupiter and its mysterious moons, the Galileo mission also becomes notable for discoveries during its journey to the gas giant. It is the first spacecraft to visit an asteroid, called Gaspra. Galileo also provides the only close observations of a comet colliding with a planet when it witnesses fragments of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 impact Jupiter. And its flight past Venus in 1990 yields fascinating infrared images of the planet's clouds.

And Juno’s work continues building on the discoveries of previous missions that visited Jupiter – Pioneer 10 and 11, and Voyager 1 and 2 in the 1970s, then the Galileo orbiter and its atmospheric probe, as well as those spacecraft who made key observations while en route to other targets (Ulysses, Cassini, and New Horizons). In turn, Juno is also preparing the way for future visitors, such as ESA’s Juice mission (JUpiter ICy moons Explorer), launched in April 2023 and scheduled to reach Jupiter in July 2031. Next to go, NASA’s Europa Clipper is scheduled to launch in October 2024, and enter orbit around Jupiter in April 2030. For Juno, exploring the full Jovian system, passing through the doughnut-shaped clouds of charged particles surrounding Europa, Io, and the other moons, testing the radiation environment, studying the dust in Jupiter’s faint rings – all this work and more will inform the mission designs, science priorities, observation strategies, and more for Europa Clipper, Juice, and others that will surely follow. Jupiter ExplorationJuno continues a lineage of discovery at the king of planets, and is helping prepare the next generation of missions bound for Jupiter.More About Jupiter ExplorationContinuing a LegacyJuno builds on the work of previous missions to Jupiter, and paves the way for its successors.
